chapter: The Latin scene and business of the 1940s-70s
title: Finances after Carnegie Hall and the 1948 jazz records
summary: He made little money; labels and Latin radio ignored him.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I haven't been able to play a club in the last five months. You mean to tell me it's not possible (unintelligible) with the record.
Who did you record it for?
I recorded for Company. But the guy was (unintelligible) ran all over me.
What happens -- I want to get back to the -- there was a moment -- you had the Carnegie Hall concert, which must have looked as if you were really going to go places.
That's what I thought, that's what I thought. I thought, this is it.
But then, a year later, you were playing for jazzmen, recording (unintelligible) in '48, right?
How did you do financially out of those kinds of things?
Well, financially I didn't make nothing with because (unintelligible). The only thing that I made there, I did good (unintelligible) label sold it to some syndicate in Chicago.

Nobody to play the Latin music. And then (unintelligible). But you got to record it different, you're getting too progressive, you know? That ain't Latin enough for your recording. What do you mean, Latin enough? That's (unintelligible). The Latin radio for seven, eight or nine years, they didn't play my records. (Inaudible.)
